title: Frog Jump II
statement:
The array `stones` holds the positions of stones in a river, in strictly increasing order, and `stones[0]` is `0`. A frog sitting on the first stone must travel to the last stone and then back to the first stone, moving only by jumping from stone to stone. Over the whole round trip, each stone may be the landing spot of at most one jump.

A jump from position `x` to position `y` has length `|x - y|`, and the cost of a round trip is the length of its longest jump. Return the smallest cost any valid round trip can have.
notes:
## Intuition

A brute force would assign every middle stone to the outward trip, the return trip or neither, and measure each choice: exponential. A lower bound shows the answer directly.

Take any three consecutive stones `stones[i - 2]`, `stones[i - 1]`, `stones[i]`. The middle one can be landed on at most once, so at least one direction never touches it. That direction has to jump across it, from a stone at or beyond `stones[i]` to one at or before `stones[i - 2]`, so some jump is at least `stones[i] - stones[i - 2]` long. The very first jump is also at least `stones[1] - stones[0]`.

The greedy route meets every one of these bounds at once: go out on stones 0, 2, 4, ... and come back on the odd ones. Each of its jumps spans exactly two neighbouring gaps (or the single first or last gap), so its cost equals the largest bound.

## Approach

1. Start `best` with the first gap, `stones[1] - stones[0]` (the whole answer when there are only two stones).
2. For every `i` from 2 to `n - 1`, compute the skip-one distance `skip = stones[i] - stones[i - 2]`.
3. If `skip` is larger than `best`, raise `best` to it.
4. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`stones = [0, 2, 5, 6, 7]`.

- `best = 2 - 0 = 2`.
- `i = 2`: `5 - 0 = 5`, so `best = 5`.
- `i = 3`: `6 - 2 = 4`, no change.
- `i = 4`: `7 - 5 = 2`, no change.

The answer is `5`: out `0 → 5 → 7`, back `7 → 6 → 2 → 0`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the stones.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- With only two stones there is no `i = 2`; the answer is the single gap, used twice.
- Visiting every stone is never worse: an extra stop only splits a jump into shorter ones.
- Do not use the largest single gap; skipping a stone doubles up two gaps.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `best` | the largest lower bound found so far, which is the answer at the end |
| `n` | number of stones |
| `i` | index of the stone a skip-one jump lands on |
| `skip` | distance from `stones[i - 2]` to `stones[i]`, a lower bound on the cost |

narration.2: Remember how many stones there are.
narration.3: The first jump out of stone 0 is at least the first gap, so start the answer there.
narration.4: Look at every stone that can be reached by skipping exactly one stone.
narration.5: Some jump must cross stones[i - 1], from stones[i] or beyond to stones[i - 2] or before, so the cost is at least this skip.
narration.6: Is this lower bound larger than the best one so far?
narration.7: Yes: the answer must be at least this skip.
narration.10: The alternating route meets every bound at once, so the largest bound is the minimum cost.
